Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on LLM activations learn to decompose representations into sparse linear combinations of learned "features," and the central question here is whether the pattern of which neurons become active or silent across training can be understood through thermodynamic analogies — specifically, whether activation sparsity behaves like a phase transition (sharp, collective, order-parameter-driven) rather than a smooth optimization convergence. The key concepts are: the L1 sparsity penalty as a proxy for a temperature-like control parameter, dead neuron phenomena as absorbing states analogous to frozen degrees of freedom, the geometry of the loss landscape as an energy landscape, and the training trajectory as a path through that landscape toward lower free-energy configurations. A critical subtlety experts hold that beginners miss: sparsity percentage is not the same as sparsity structure — a network can hit a target activation rate while encoding completely incoherent features, and the thermodynamic interest is precisely in when and why coherent, semantically interpretable features crystallize as stable attractors rather than diffuse across many weakly-active neurons. The deeper worry is that most empirical SAE work tracks loss curves and reconstruction fidelity, but these are bulk thermodynamic quantities that can remain smooth even while the microscopic feature landscape undergoes sharp structural reorganization — meaning standard training diagnostics are nearly blind to the most interesting dynamics.

The L1 penalty breaks neuron symmetry through a sparsifying pressure that is direction-sensitive in activation space: for a neuron with weight vector w and activation h, the gradient of λ|h| with respect to w is λ·sign(h)·x, meaning the penalty pushes weight vectors toward directions where most inputs produce exactly zero activation — a property that favors axis-aligned or near-axis-aligned solutions in the residual stream basis. Unlike L2, which treats all directions equally (preserving rotational symmetry), L1 creates a free-energy well around sparse solutions that is asymmetric under rotation: rotating two neurons' weight vectors into a superposition generically increases their combined L1 cost because the new features activate on more inputs, even if reconstruction loss is unchanged. This is the core symmetry-breaking: L1 penalizes overlap with the data manifold, so neurons specialize by retreating to directions that are orthogonal to as much of the activation distribution as possible. However — and this is where experts get nervous — the broken symmetry is only local: Anthropic's early SAE work (Bricken et al., 2023) on one-layer MLP neurons found that different random seeds reliably recover qualitatively similar monosemantic features for high-frequency concepts, but for mid-frequency or polysemantic input regions, feature splits vary substantially across runs, indicating a rough free-energy landscape with many nearly-degenerate minima. The implication for uniqueness is stark: the L1 penalty guarantees a sparse solution exists and is preferred over dense ones, but it provides no convexity guarantee in the joint (encoder, decoder) space — the SAE objective is bilinear, and the number of equivalent sparse decompositions of a fixed activation distribution scales combinatorially with dictionary size, a problem directly analogous to the non-identifiability of independent component analysis without additional distributional assumptions.

The cleanest empirical signature is bipartite feature matching under a permutation-invariant similarity metric: take two SAEs trained identically except for seed, compute the cosine similarity matrix between all pairs of decoder vectors, find the maximum-weight bipartite matching, and examine the distribution of matched-pair similarities. Anthropic's SAE work and independent replications (e.g., Cunningham et al., 2023 on residual stream SAEs) find that high-frequency, high-activation features match at cosine similarity >0.9 across seeds, while the long tail of rare features shows matches clustering around 0.4–0.6 — which is above chance but far below identity, the precise signature of a rough landscape with a shared global basin for common structure and fragmented local minima for rare structure. A subtler diagnostic is functional equivalence under interchange: replace SAE-A's features with SAE-B's matched features in a downstream circuit analysis (e.g., patching into an attention head's input) and measure whether causal effect sizes are preserved; if they are, the solutions are functionally identical even if geometrically rotated. The distinction does matter for interpretability, but asymmetrically: for the goal of finding which concepts a model represents, near-equivalent solutions are fine — both decompositions expose the same high-frequency monosemantic features. But for the goal of circuit-level mechanistic analysis — tracing how feature X causally produces feature Y across layers — non-uniqueness is poisonous, because a causal graph built on one decomposition may have edges that vanish or reverse under a different but equally valid decomposition, giving the illusion of mechanism where there is only a choice of basis. The deeper issue, largely unaddressed in current literature, is that there is no agreed-upon equivalence class definition: two SAEs could agree on all features above frequency 10⁻³ and disagree entirely on the bottom decade of the frequency distribution, and current evals (L0, reconstruction loss, interpretability scores) would rate them as essentially identical despite having meaningfully different implied circuit structures for rare behaviors.

The most principled candidate for a canonical decomposition comes from independent component analysis theory: a decomposition is unique (up to sign and permutation) if and only if at most one source is Gaussian — meaning the data distribution itself must be sufficiently non-Gaussian in enough directions to pin down the basis. For LLM residual streams, there is suggestive but incomplete evidence that this condition is approximately met: activation distributions are heavily kurtotic and skewed (Anthropic's scaling monosemanticity work notes that individual feature activations follow approximately exponential or Laplace distributions), which in principle provides enough non-Gaussianity to constrain the decomposition, but the joint distribution across thousands of dimensions has never been rigorously characterized well enough to invoke ICA uniqueness theorems. A second approach appeals to model geometry rather than data statistics: if the model's weights implement a specific computational structure — say, attention heads that read and write along fixed directions in residual stream space — then the "true" features are those aligned with those computational directions, and the canonical decomposition is the one whose dictionary vectors best predict the weight matrices of downstream components, not just the activation distribution. This is the implicit logic behind recent work like RAVEL (Huang et al., 2024) and geometry-based feature identification, which find that causally active directions in residual space are more stable across SAE seeds than purely reconstructive features — suggesting model geometry provides a harder constraint than reconstruction alone. The uncomfortable answer for thermodynamic framing is that canonicality likely requires breaking the problem into two separate optimizations: first find directions that are causally stable under intervention (pinned by model weights), then find a sparse decomposition of the remaining variance — but this sequential approach has no clean loss function and would require solving a causal discovery problem before the representational one, reversing the usual workflow entirely.

The initialization hypothesis is partially supported but requires careful decomposition: weight matrices at initialization are random and impose no privileged directions, but gradient flow during training breaks this symmetry progressively, and there is strong evidence from grokking experiments (Nanda et al., 2023) and phase transition work that discrete computational structures — modular arithmetic circuits, induction heads — crystallize at specific training steps rather than emerging gradually, suggesting the causal directions are created during training rather than latent from the start. The more defensible claim is that once a computational structure crystallizes, it anchors specific directions in residual space that become load-bearing for downstream components, and subsequent training then recruits activation statistics to align with those directions — meaning weight geometry leads and activation distribution follows, not the reverse. This has a direct implication for SAEs: if you train an SAE on checkpoints at 10%, 50%, and 100% of training (as Anthropic has begun doing in their updates on features across training), you should find that the causally stable features appear abruptly coincident with phase transitions in the underlying model, while the reconstructively convenient features drift smoothly — and conflating these two populations is precisely the error that makes it hard to answer whether SAEs discover or impose. The discovery-vs-imposition question then resolves into a contingent empirical one rather than a philosophical one: SAEs discover structure when their dictionary vectors align with weight-pinned directions that preexist the SAE's training, and they impose structure when they carve up high-variance activation regions that have no privileged computational basis — and current SAEs almost certainly do both simultaneously with no mechanism to separate the two populations. The sharpest version of the worry is that L1 regularization, by penalizing activation frequency uniformly, is blind to causal load: a direction that carries 90% of the causal effect on downstream components but activates rarely will receive the same sparsity pressure as a causally inert direction with identical activation frequency, meaning the penalty actively works against discovering the most important structure.

The natural alternative is a causally-weighted sparsity penalty of the form λ(w)·|h|, where λ(w) is inversely proportional to the causal influence of direction w on downstream components — operationalized as the Frobenius norm of the projection of downstream weight matrices onto w, so directions that are heavily read by attention heads or MLCs incur lower sparsity cost and are allowed to activate more freely. This is structurally analogous to importance-weighted pruning in the network compression literature (cf. optimal brain damage, LeCun et al. 1990; more recently Wanda, Sun et al. 2023), but inverted: instead of pruning low-importance weights, you're protecting high-causal-load directions from sparsification pressure. The thermodynamic analogy is precise and illuminating: standard L1 is an entropic pressure that treats all microstates (feature activations) as equally costly, pushing toward maximum sparsity as a uniform temperature would push toward maximum entropy subject to an energy constraint — but causally-weighted L1 introduces a non-uniform chemical potential, where certain directions have lower effective temperature and can maintain occupancy without thermodynamic penalty, analogous to a Bose-Einstein condensate where low-energy modes accumulate population that a uniform-temperature system would distribute away. A concrete implementation would use indirect readout weights: for each SAE dictionary vector dᵢ, compute a causal weight cᵢ = Σⱼ ||Wⱼ dᵢ||² summed over all downstream weight matrices Wⱼ, then set λᵢ = λ₀ / (1 + αcᵢ), reducing sparsity pressure proportionally to causal load — this requires one forward pass through the model's weight matrices per SAE training step, which is computationally cheap relative to activation collection. The unresolved difficulty is causal credit assignment across layers: a direction in layer 8 may be causally important only because it feeds a layer-9 direction that feeds a layer-12 output head, and the local readout weight norm at layer 8 understates its true causal load by ignoring the transitive chain — meaning the thermodynamic analogy breaks down unless you propagate causal weights backward through the model's computational graph, which is essentially running a causal version of backpropagation before SAE training even begins.

The distinction does partially collapse, but not completely, and the residual difference is both real and important: gradient-based methods (saliency maps, integrated gradients, SAGE) identify which input directions causally influence a specific output, but they do so conditional on a fixed input and output, producing a different attribution vector for every (input, output) pair — they describe the local geometry of the loss landscape at a point, not a reusable dictionary of computational primitives. SAEs add exactly one thing that gradient methods cannot: amortized, input-independent basis vectors — the decoder dictionary is trained to be a universal sparse basis for the activation distribution, meaning you get the same feature set regardless of which input you're analyzing, which is a precondition for statements like "this circuit uses feature F across many contexts" rather than "this input activates this direction." The thermodynamic analogy is sharp here: gradient methods give you the force at a specific point in phase space, while SAEs attempt to identify the stable attractors of the representation — the free-energy minima that the model's activations repeatedly fall into across the data distribution, which are properties of the landscape topology rather than any local gradient. Concretely, Anthropic's work on features in Claude (2024) finds features that activate on highly heterogeneous input sets — the "Assistant" token feature activating across thousands of syntactically unrelated contexts — which no single gradient computation would reveal because no single input exposes the full scope of the feature's activation distribution. However, this advantage is contingent on the SAE having correctly identified a true stable attractor rather than a convenient reconstruction basis, which returns us to the earlier problem: if the dictionary vector doesn't correspond to a weight-pinned direction, the "universal" basis is universal only with respect to the activation distribution, not with respect to the model's computational structure, and gradient methods applied to individual inputs would actually be more causally accurate than the SAE feature, just less convenient.

The principled combination exists and can be stated precisely: for each SAE feature with decoder vector dᵢ, compute the causal consistency score as the correlation between (a) the feature's activation coefficient hᵢ(x) across inputs x and (b) the gradient projection ∇xL · dᵢ onto that same direction — a genuine universal attractor should activate strongly exactly when the model's output is causally sensitive to perturbations along dᵢ, while an activation-distribution artifact will show high hᵢ with near-zero gradient projection because the direction is frequently occupied but causally inert. This test has a partial empirical precedent in activation patching consistency checks (Wang et al., IOI circuit 2022; Conmy et al., ACDC 2023): features that survive causal tracing — where patching the feature's activation changes downstream behavior — form a strict subset of features identified by reconstruction-based SAEs, with the remainder being what Conmy et al. effectively call "dead ends" in the circuit graph, directions the model encodes but never reads. The thermodynamic interpretation is that genuine attractors are thermodynamically coupled to the output — they sit at the bottom of free-energy wells that are load-bearing in the sense that displacing them costs output probability, whereas artifact features sit in wells that are geometrically stable but thermodynamically isolated from the output manifold, like a metastable crystal that never melts but also never conducts. A concrete validation protocol would collect N~10,000 inputs, compute both hᵢ and ∇L·dᵢ for each, fit a linear regression of gradient projection onto activation coefficient, and threshold on R² > 0.3 as a minimum causal consistency criterion — features below threshold are candidates for pruning from the dictionary as activation-distribution artifacts. The significant unresolved problem is nonlinearity: gradient projections capture only first-order causal sensitivity, so features involved in threshold-gating computations (where causal influence is near-zero until activation crosses a boundary) will fail the consistency test despite being genuinely causally important — meaning the validation protocol systematically misclassifies features that implement discontinuous or highly nonlinear computations, which may be precisely the features doing the most interesting work.
